summary_html: **Healthcare encounters** that reveal suspected abuse or neglect trigger reporting obligations. Federal law governs mandatory reporting in federal facilities and coordination with state systems.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — state reporter systems and protections  
- **Victims of Child Abuse Act (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — mandates in federal settings, CAC coordination

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Elizabeth Lawson v. Patricia Halpern-Reiss and Central Vermont Medical Center
key_cases.holding: The Court recognized a common-law private right of action for a medical provider's unjustified disclosure of treatment information, but affirmed judgment for the hospital because the disclosure fell within the exception for mitigating an imminent and serious threat.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Vermont authority on the scope and limits of a medical provider's disclosure of treatment information to third parties including law enforcement.
key_cases.quote: no reasonable factfinder could determine that the disclosure was for any purpose other than to mitigate the threat of imminent and serious harm to plaintiff and the public

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for the defendants was affirmed because during the relevant period the newborn was held by the hospital for medical reasons rather than by the child-welfare agency, so no Fourth or Fourteenth Amendment violation arose from the retention.
key_cases.relevance: Kia P. separates a medical hold arising from a positive newborn toxicology screen from state child-protective custody, which determines which constitutional rules apply.
key_cases.quote: Mora was held by the Hospital for medical reasons, not concerns about possible parental mistreatment and CWA policies

key_cases.holding: The substantiation and registry placement were reversed because they had to be supported by sufficient evidence known to DCF at the time of substantiation, and the petitioner's later admissions could not retroactively justify them.
key_cases.relevance: A hospital report of a parent's overdose triggered the investigation, and K.R. limits how far that medical information can carry a finding.
key_cases.quote: However, after-acquired evidence cannot salvage a substantiation that was not supported by sufficient evidence in the first place.

key_cases.case_name: Willis S. Sheldon, Individually and as Administrator of the Estate of Dezirae Sheldon v. Nicholas Ruggiero
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for a DCF administrative reviewer was affirmed because the mandated-reporter duty under 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a) is triggered only by reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused, and a repetitious allegation adding nothing new did not supply it.
key_cases.relevance: Dezirae's injuries came to DCF through a hospital presentation, and the opinion traces how medical findings feed the § 4915 investigation.
key_cases.quote: In this context, as a matter of law, defendant did not have reasonable cause to make a report.

search_keywords: Vermont Department for Children and Families

state_agency.name: Vermont Department for Children and Families, Family Services Division

mandatory_reporters: Health care providers, including physicians, surgeons, osteopaths, chiropractors, physician assistants, resident physicians, interns, hospital administrators, registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, medical examiners, emergency medical personnel, dentists, psychologists, and pharmacists — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(1)

School district and approved or recognized independent school employees, and contracted student-services providers, including superintendents, headmasters, teachers, student teachers, school librarians, principals, and guidance counselors — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(2)
Agency of Human Services employees, contractors, and grantees who have contact with clients — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(7)
Camp owners (“camp” includes any residential or nonresidential recreational program, 33 V.S.A. § 4913(b)) — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(9)
Members of the clergy, except information received while acting as a spiritual advisor in a confidential communication (33 V.S.A. § 4913(j)) — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(12)
Employees of the Office of the Child, Youth, and Family Advocate — 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a)(13)
reporting_details: Vermont is not a universal-reporting state: the 13 categories of mandated reporters listed in 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a) must report to DCF within 24 hours of the time the information was first received or observed, and any other concerned person may report voluntarily (33 V.S.A. § 4913(c), (e)).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 72 hours to begin an assessment or investigation
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the report, once accepted as a valid allegation and there is sufficient information to proceed
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The Commissioner may waive the 72-hour requirement only when necessary to locate the child or to ensure the safety of the child or social worker (33 V.S.A. § 4915(b)).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days (assessment track); no statutory deadline (investigation track)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: An assessment may be extended only upon written justification by the Department and not beyond 60 days total (33 V.S.A. § 4915a(b)); Vermont sets no completion deadline for the investigation track (33 V.S.A. § 4915b).
